cards.q: Declare `pq`, a min-heap of `int`.
cards.a: The default `priority_queue<int>` is a max-heap. To pass `greater<int>` you must also spell out the container, `vector<int>`.

cards.q: With `using P = pair<int, int>;`, declare a lambda `cmp` and a heap `pq` so the pair with the smallest `.second` is on top.
cards.a: A comparator returning true means `a` sinks below `b`, so `>` gives a min-heap. `decltype(cmp)` names the type, and C++17 also needs `cmp` passed to the constructor.
cards.code: auto cmp = [](const P& a, const P& b) { return a.second > b.second; }; priority_queue, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);

cards.q: Store in `int i` the index of the first element of sorted `v` that is not less than `x`.
cards.a: `lower_bound` returns an iterator, and subtracting `v.begin()` turns it into an index. If every element is smaller, `i` equals `v.size()`.
cards.code: int i = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - v.begin();

cards.q: Set `bool has` to whether key `k` is in map `m`, without modifying `m`.
cards.a: `m[k]` inserts a zero for a missing key, so testing with it grows the map.

cards.q: In what order does a range-for visit a `map`, and in what order an `unordered_map`?
cards.a: `map` goes in ascending key order. `unordered_map` order is unspecified and can change after a rehash.

cards.q: For `map<int, int> m`, why write `m.lower_bound(k)` and not `std::lower_bound` over `m.begin()` to `m.end()`?
cards.a: The member function descends the tree in O(log n). `std::lower_bound` needs random-access iterators to be fast, so on a `map` it walks step by step in O(n). It also compares whole `pair` elements, so it would need a custom comparator.

cards.q: For `set<int> s`, set `ans` to the largest element `<= x`, leaving `ans` unchanged if there is none.
cards.a: `upper_bound` gives the first element `> x`, so the one before it is the floor. Check against `s.begin()`, because `prev(s.begin())` is undefined.
cards.code:
auto it = s.upper_bound(x);
if (it != s.begin()) ans = *prev(it);

cards.q: Insert `x` into `set<int> s` and set `bool added` to whether `x` was new.
cards.a: `insert` returns `pair<iterator, bool>`. The `bool` is false if an equal element already existed.

cards.q: Set `int lo` and `int hi` to the smallest and largest values in non-empty `multiset<int> ms`.
cards.a: `set` and `multiset` stay sorted, so the two ends hold the extremes. Use `rbegin()`, because `end()` points past the last element.

cards.q: Remove exactly one copy of `x` from `multiset<int> ms`, where `x` is known to be present.
cards.a: `ms.erase(x)` removes every copy, because the value overload erases all matches. The iterator overload erases one, and passing `end()` is undefined.

cards.q: Erase every entry of `map<int, int> m` with value 0, in a single loop over iterators.
cards.a: `erase` invalidates `it` and returns the next valid iterator. Advance either by that assignment or by `it++`, never both.

cards.q: Delete every element equal to `x` from `vector<int> v` in O(n).
cards.a: `remove` shifts the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end, without changing the size. `erase` then cuts off the tail.

cards.q: Declare `dp`, a table of zeros with `m + 1` rows and `n + 1` columns.
cards.a: The second argument is one row, and the outer vector copies it `m + 1` times. `vector<int>(n + 1)` is already zero-filled.

cards.q: How many elements do `vector<int> a(3, 7);` and `vector<int> b{3, 7};` hold?
cards.a: `a` holds three 7s. `b` holds two elements, 3 and 7, because braces prefer the initializer-list constructor.

cards.q: After `vector<int> v; v.reserve(10);`, is `v[0] = 1;` valid?
cards.a: No, it is undefined. `reserve` only sets capacity, so the size is still 0, and `resize(10)` is what creates elements.

cards.q: Why does `auto& x = flags[0];` not compile for `vector<bool> flags`?
cards.a: `vector<bool>` packs elements into bits, so `operator[]` returns a temporary proxy object, not a `bool&`. A non-const reference cannot bind to a temporary.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `1`. `auto` deduces the proxy, which still refers to the bit. Write `bool x = flags[0];` to get a real copy.

cards.q: Why is the last line undefined behaviour?
cards.a: `push_back` may reallocate, which invalidates every reference, pointer and iterator into the vector. Take them after the last insertion, or hold an index instead.

cards.q: In `map`, `set` and `list`, which iterators does an insert or an erase invalidate?
cards.a: An insert invalidates none. An erase invalidates only iterators to the erased element.

cards.q: What does a rehash of an `unordered_map` invalidate?
cards.a: All iterators, but not pointers or references to elements. Any insert can trigger a rehash, so do not hold an iterator across one.

cards.q: Append the pair `(1, 2)` to `vector<pair<int, int>> v` using `emplace_back`.
cards.a: `emplace_back` forwards constructor arguments, so it takes no braces: `v.emplace_back({1, 2})` does not compile. `push_back` takes an object, so `v.push_back({1, 2})` is the braced form.

cards.q:
With `using P = pair;`, sort `vector

v` by `.second` ascending, using a lambda.
cards.a: For `sort`, returning true means `a` comes first. That is the opposite reading from `priority_queue`, where `>` gives a min-heap.

cards.q: Why is this comparator a bug?
cards.a: A comparator must be a strict weak ordering, so `cmp(x, x)` must be false. `<=` breaks that, which makes the behaviour undefined, and `sort` can run out of bounds.

cards.q: Sort `vector<int> v` in descending order using a standard function object.
cards.a: `sort` takes an object, so write `greater<int>()` with parentheses. `priority_queue` takes a type, so there it is `greater<int>` without them.

cards.q: What does `stable_sort` guarantee that `sort` does not?
cards.a: Elements that compare equal keep their original relative order. That lets you sort by a secondary key first and by the primary key second.

cards.q: Rearrange `vector<int> v` in average O(n) so that `v[k]` holds the value it would have if `v` were sorted.
cards.a: Elements before `v[k]` are `<=` it and elements after are `>=` it, but neither side is sorted. The middle argument is an iterator, not the index `k`.

cards.q: Put the `k` smallest elements of `vector<int> v` at the front in sorted order, in O(n log k).
cards.a: The rest of the vector is left in unspecified order. If the front `k` need not be sorted, `nth_element` is cheaper.

cards.q: Turn `vector<int> v` into its sorted distinct values.
cards.a: `unique` only collapses adjacent duplicates, so sort first. It returns the new logical end and leaves the size alone, so `erase` must cut the tail.

cards.q: Sum `vector<int> v` into `long long total` so that large sums do not overflow.
cards.a: The type of the third argument is the type of the running sum, so a plain `0` adds in `int` and overflows. `accumulate` is in `<numeric>`.

cards.q: Reverse `string s` in place using the STL.
cards.a: `reverse` takes an iterator range and returns `void`, so its result cannot be assigned. `string` has no `.reverse()` member.

cards.q: Set `int mx` to the largest value in non-empty `vector<int> v`.
cards.a: `max_element` returns an iterator, so dereference it with `*`. On an empty range it returns `end()`, and dereferencing that is undefined.

cards.q: Set `int i` to the index of the smallest value in non-empty `vector<int> v`.
cards.a: Subtract `v.begin()` to turn the iterator into an index. On ties you get the first smallest element.

cards.q: Using `next_permutation`, set `int cnt` to the number of distinct orderings of `vector<int> v`.
cards.a: Sort first, because `next_permutation` returns false after the largest ordering, wherever you started. `do`-`while` counts the starting ordering too.

cards.q: `vector<int> parent(n)` needs `parent[i] == i` for every `i`. Set that with one STL call.
cards.a: `iota` is in `<numeric>` and writes consecutive values starting at the third argument. It overwrites existing elements, so the vector must already be sized.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `16843009`, which is `0x01010101`. `memset` writes bytes, so only 0 and -1 give the expected `int` value. Use `fill` for anything else.

cards.q: Why does this not clear the whole array?
cards.a: `a` decays to a pointer, so `sizeof(a)` is the pointer size, not the array size. Use `n * sizeof(int)` or `fill(a, a + n, 0)`.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `cde`. The arguments are a start index and a length, not an end index.

cards.q: Set `string t` to the characters of `s` from index `l` to index `r`, both inclusive.
cards.a: The second argument is a length, so inclusive bounds need the `+ 1`.

cards.q: Set `bool has` to whether `string s` contains `"ab"`.
cards.a: `string::find` returns an index, or `string::npos` if there is no match. It is not an iterator, so do not compare it with `s.end()`.

cards.q: Convert `string s` to `int x`, then convert `x` back to `string t`.
cards.a: `stoi` throws `invalid_argument` when no digits can be read and `out_of_range` when the value does not fit. Use `stoll` for `long long`.
cards.code:
int x = stoi(s);
string t = to_string(x);

cards.q: What does `stoi("12abc")` return?
cards.a: 12. It parses the longest valid numeric prefix and ignores the rest, throwing only if there is no such prefix.

cards.q: Set `int d` to the numeric value of digit character `c`.
cards.a: Digit characters have consecutive codes, so subtracting `'0'` gives 0 to 9. `int d = c;` would give the character code, such as 48 for `'0'`.

cards.q: Set `char c` to the letter at 0-based position `i` of the lowercase alphabet.
cards.a: `'a' + i` is an `int`, and assigning it to `char` turns it back into a letter. `c - 'a'` is the reverse.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `98`. Arithmetic promotes `char` to `int`, so `cout` prints a number. `char('a' + 1)` prints `b`.

cards.q: Read one whole line from standard input, spaces included, into a new `string line`.
cards.a: `cin >> s` stops at whitespace. `getline` reads up to the newline and discards it.

cards.q: The input is `5` on one line and `hello` on the next. What does `line` hold?
cards.a: An empty string. `cin >> n` leaves the newline unread and `getline` stops there at once, so call `cin.ignore();` before it.

cards.q: Split `string line` on whitespace into `vector<string> words` using a `stringstream`.
cards.a: `ss >> word` skips any run of whitespace and fails at the end of the stream, which ends the loop. `stringstream` is in `<sstream>`.

cards.q: Store the product of `int a` and `int b` in `long long p` without overflow.
cards.a: `long long p = a * b;` still overflows, because `a * b` is computed in `int` before the conversion. Making the first operand `long long` widens the whole product.

cards.q: Declare `int mid` halfway between `int lo` and `int hi`, safe from overflow.
cards.a: `(lo + hi) / 2` overflows when the sum passes `INT_MAX`. `hi - lo` stays in range for `0 <= lo <= hi`.

cards.q: Summing 1e5 values of up to 1e9 each, which type does the total need?
cards.a: `long long`. The total can reach 1e14, while `int` stops near 2.1e9 and `long long` near 9.2e18.

cards.q: Set `long long best` to the largest `long long` value, using `numeric_limits`.
cards.a: `max()` is a function, so keep the parentheses. For `int`, the shorter `INT_MAX` from `<climits>` does the same job.

cards.q: Why does `max(a, b)` not compile when `a` is `long long` and `b` is `int`?
cards.a: `max` takes two arguments of one deduced type `T`, and here the deduction conflicts. Write `max<long long>(a, b)` or cast `b`.

cards.q: Set `int best` to the smallest of `a`, `b` and `c` with a single call to `min`.
cards.a: The braces build an `initializer_list`, which has its own overload. `min(a, b, c)` is wrong, because its third parameter is a comparator.

cards.q: What happens when this runs?
cards.a: `v.size()` is unsigned, so `v.size() - 1` wraps to a huge value and the loop reads out of bounds. Fix it with `int n = v.size();` and `i < n - 1`.

cards.q: Set `int ones` to the number of set bits in `int x`, using a compiler builtin.
cards.a: It takes an `unsigned int`, and `__builtin_popcountll` is the 64-bit form. Builtins are GCC and Clang extensions, not standard C++.

cards.q: Set `int tz` to the number of trailing zero bits in nonzero `int x`, using a compiler builtin.
cards.a: The result is undefined for `x == 0`, so guard that case. `__builtin_ctzll` is the 64-bit form.

cards.q: Declare `bitset<1000> b`, set bit 5, and store the number of set bits in `int ones`.
cards.a: The size is a compile-time constant. `b[i]` or `b.test(i)` reads a bit, and `b.to_string()` gives the binary text.

cards.q: With `deque<int> dq`, add `x` at the front, add `y` at the back, then remove the front element.
cards.a: Both ends are O(1), and `dq[i]` gives random access, which `queue` does not. Read the ends with `dq.front()` and `dq.back()`.

cards.q: Move the top of `stack<int> st` into `int x`, removing it from the stack.
cards.a: `pop()` returns `void`, so read `top()` first.

cards.q: Move the next element of `queue<int> q` into `int x`, removing it from the queue.
cards.a: `queue` uses `front()`, not `top()`; only `stack` and `priority_queue` have `top()`. Its `pop()` also returns `void`.

cards.q: Declare `cnt`, a fixed-size `array` of 26 `int` zeros.
cards.a: The empty braces zero it, while a local `array<int, 26> cnt;` holds garbage. Unlike a C array it compares with `==` and `<`, so it can be a `map` key.

cards.q: How does `<` compare two `pair<int, int>` values?
cards.a: By `first`, then by `second` when the firsts are equal. So `sort` needs no comparator for that order, and `priority_queue` puts the largest `first` on top.

cards.q: Declare `tuple<int, int, string> t` holding 1, 2 and `"a"`, then read its last field into `string s`.
cards.a: The index in `get<2>` is a template argument, so it must be a compile-time constant. A loop variable will not work.
cards.code:
tuple<int, int, string> t = {1, 2, "a"};
string s = get<2>(t);

cards.q: Unpack `pair<int, int> p` into new variables `a` and `b` in one line.
cards.a: Structured bindings need C++17. Plain `auto` copies, while `auto& [a, b] = p;` binds to the original.

cards.q: Add every value of `map<string, int> m` to `int total`, using structured bindings named `k` and `v` and no copies.
cards.a: Each element is a `pair<const string, int>`. `const auto&` avoids copying the string key on every step.
cards.code: for (const auto& [k, v] : m) total += v;

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `1`. `x` is a copy, so the vector is unchanged. Write `for (int& x : v)` to modify elements.

cards.q: Add the length of every string in `vector<string> words` to `int total`, without copying any string.
cards.a: `auto w` copies each string. Use `const auto&` for anything larger than a small scalar that you only read.
cards.code: for (const auto& w : words) total += w.size();

cards.q: Given child lists `vector<vector<int>> adj`, define a recursive lambda `dfs` returning the size of the subtree at `u`, then store `dfs(0)` in `int total`.
cards.a: `auto dfs` does not compile, because the variable cannot appear in its own initialiser before its type is known. `function<int(int)>` names the type up front.

cards.q: What does storing a recursive lambda in `function<int(int)>` cost?
cards.a: Every call is an indirect call through type erasure that the compiler usually cannot inline, and constructing the `function` may allocate. That is fine for most interview code, but a named function is faster in hot recursion.

cards.q: Why must this lambda capture with `[&]`, not `[=]`?
cards.a: `[=]` copies `f` before `f` is initialised, which is undefined behaviour. `[&]` stores a reference, and `f` is ready by the time the lambda runs.

cards.q: Without `function`, define a recursive generic lambda `fact` that takes itself as `self`, then store `fact(fact, 5)` in `int ans`.
cards.a: The lambda receives itself as an argument, so there is no `function` overhead. The `-> int` is needed here, because the return type cannot be deduced through the recursive call.

cards.q: What are the two problems with this by-value `seen` in a recursive `dfs`?
cards.a: Each call copies the whole vector, which costs O(n) per call. Marks made by a deeper call are also lost when it returns, so declare `vector<int>& seen`.

cards.q: Write `struct PairHash` so that `unordered_map<pair<int, int>, int, PairHash> m` compiles, combining `hash<int>` of both fields with a multiplier of 31, then declare `m`.
cards.a: `std::hash` has no `pair` specialisation, so the map needs a hasher as its third template argument. `operator()` must be `const`. A `map<pair<int, int>, int>` needs no hasher at all, at O(log n) per access.

cards.q: Define `struct ListNode` with `int val`, `ListNode* next`, and a constructor `ListNode(int x)` that uses an initialiser list.
cards.a: Forgetting `next(nullptr)` leaves `next` uninitialised, so the first walk of the list can crash. Use `ListNode dummy(0);` for a stack node and `new ListNode(0)` for a heap node.
